content:
Andy Robertson believes Liverpool’s prospects of mounting a serious Premier League title challenge under new head coach Arne Slot will depend heavily on whether they can become more reliable defensively. Slot has begun his time in charge with two league matches and two clean sheets, an ideal platform for a team hoping to compete with Manchester City and Arsenal near the top of the table. Liverpool’s early fixtures against Ipswich Town and Brentford did not produce any goals against them, allowing the new manager to make a strong first impression. However, Robertson knows the next assignment will provide a much clearer measure of their progress. Liverpool travel to Old Trafford to face Manchester United, a fixture that usually brings greater pressure, higher intensity and more dangerous attacking moments than the ones they have faced so far. For that reason, the left-back views Sunday’s match as an important test of whether the defensive improvement is genuine and sustainable.

handle the threat posed by United, Robertson suggested, and Liverpool can take confidence that they are moving in the right direction. He said the opening two performances had given the squad exactly what they would have wanted from a defensive point of view: two matches without conceding. Still, he stressed that this cannot be treated as a short-term achievement. The aim now is to keep restricting opponents, first by reducing the number of opportunities Manchester United are able to create and then by carrying that same discipline into the matches that follow the international break. Robertson’s comments point to a wider recognition inside the squad that Liverpool’s title push last season was undermined not simply by occasional bad results, but by the amount of work they allowed opponents to give their defence and goalkeeper. Even when they were still in contention, they were often giving up more chances than their main rivals.

Looking back at the previous campaign, Robertson noted that Liverpool conceded 41 goals across 38 league games as they finished third. That was seven more than champions Manchester City allowed and 12 more than Arsenal, who ended the season as runners-up. Those numbers, in his view, help explain why Liverpool eventually fell away. A side can survive spells of defensive vulnerability for a time, especially if its attack is productive, but repeated exposure tends to catch up with any team over the course of a title race. Robertson said that when a team consistently allows opponents opportunities, there will inevitably be matches in which those chances are converted and points are dropped. That, he suggested, is what happened to Liverpool last season. The early evidence under Slot has been encouraging, but Robertson’s message is clear: clean sheets must become a habit, not a brief opening flourish, if Liverpool are to stay close to the very best. P.S. In short, Robertson sees defensive control as central to Liverpool’s hopes of turning a promising start into a genuine title challenge.
